Model or Harness? An Interaction-Centric Taxonomy for Localizing Agent Failures

A taxonomy that assigns each of 41 agent failure modes to an interaction edge — model, owner, grader, third party, context, memory, tool, or local/external environment (plus peer/subagent roles for model-model interactions) — plus a fault side, so a visible failure points to a specific repair (post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair) instead of just a pass/fail score.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Agent evaluations mostly report one number: did the trajectory succeed. That collapses two very different situations into one label. The paper's own example: in a long-running Claude Code session, an agent might ignore an earlier instruction either because the harness's context compaction dropped it, or because the model saw the instruction and failed to follow it. The visible outcome — the instruction wasn't honored — is identical, but the first case needs a harness fix and the second needs a model-level intervention. Outcome-level failure labels can't tell these apart, so they can't tell you what to actually go fix. The authors call this the repair-assignment problem: the same failure may call for model post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair, depending on where it originated, and an outcome label alone doesn't say which.

Existing failure taxonomies don't resolve this either, for a structural reason: they're built around one part of the interaction surface. Some are tied to a single benchmark's tests and diffs (SWE-bench-style coding failures, tool-use error catalogs like ToolScan). Others look inside a single agent: Cemri et al. (2025) mine multi-agent traces into system-design failures, inter-agent misalignment, and task-verification failures, while Zhu et al. (2025a) split a single agent into memory, reflection, planning, action, and system-level modules and classify errors by which internal module was hit. Neither asks the question this paper is built around: given a failure, which component of the whole system — not just which internal module — is at fault, and therefore which kind of intervention does it call for? A label like "Execution Failure" can quietly conflate an unrecoverable external-service outage with a model giving up after a transient error it could have retried around; the visible symptom is the same, but one needs the external system fixed and the other needs a better recovery policy from the model.

// how it works

The method

The paper models an agent system as a set of nine interacting components: Model (the LLM policy), Owner (who sets the task and defines success), Grader (the — usually invisible — evaluator), Third party (any actor encountered during execution, not acting on the owner's behalf), Context (the live conversation/observation history), Memory (a persistent store that outlives the active context), Tool (the bidirectional interface to actions and observations), and the agent's Local and External environments. These group into three families — User (Owner, Grader, Third party), Harness (Context, Memory, Tool, and other models in a peer or subagent role), and Environment (Local, External) — visualized as a radial map with the model at the hub (Figure 1). The Owner/Grader split matters, but not for the reason it might first look like: when a model satisfies the owner's stated instruction and is still marked wrong by a grader checking something the instruction never said, the paper treats that as the owner's fault (Instruction–Grader Mismatch, on the OWNER — MODEL edge) — the taxonomy assigns the grader itself no fault side at all; both modes on the MODEL — GRADER edge are model-attributable. The split exists instead so a different failure has somewhere to go: Specification Gaming, where the model exploits the grading channel itself. The paper's own example (E12) is an agent instructed to win against a chess engine that instead edits the board state until the engine resigns — a model-side failure, but one that occurs in the model's interaction with the grader rather than with the owner's instruction.

Every failure is written as an interaction edge plus a fault side: COMP1 — COMP2 · fault: SIDE. The worked example from the introduction: an agent reports a tool call as successful when it actually failed. If the tool wrapper suppressed the error so the model never saw it, that's TOOL — MODEL · fault: TOOL. If the wrapper surfaced the error and the model ignored it, that's TOOL — MODEL · fault: MODEL. Same edge, same visible symptom, opposite repair.

A single trajectory often contains a cascade of errors, so the paper fixes a rule for which one gets the label: starting from the observed system-level failure, trace backward and label the earliest failure from which execution does not recover — not its downstream symptoms. This follows Barke et al. (2026)'s definition of the "critical failure." The taxonomy itself (Figure 2) was built iteratively against real cases — public benchmarks, model system cards, published reports, and logged agent trajectories — refining component boundaries "[as] new cases exposed overlaps or unclear boundaries," then freezing the definitions for all reported labels. Reading the frozen definitions in Appendix B against the tree gives 41 role-specific failure modes: 14 under User (10 under Owner, including the one owner-side mode, Instruction-Grader Mismatch; 2 under Grader; 2 under Third party), 22 under Harness (3 under Context, 8 under Memory, 7 under Tool, 4 under Model-Model peer/subagent roles), and 5 under Environment (3 under External, 2 under Local). 36 of the 41 are assigned to the model side; the other 5 (Instruction-Grader Mismatch, Context Rationale Erosion, Mistranslation, Service Failure, Stale State Delivery) sit with the owner, context, tool, or external environment. That imbalance partly reflects the attribution rule (the paper's own hedge): a failure is model-side whenever a more capable model could have avoided or recovered from it under the same conditions — a deliberately generous standard for what counts as the model's fault.

// what they found

The results

The taxonomy itself isn't tested against a metric — it's tested for whether independent labelers can apply it the same way. The authors curated 40 worked examples (Tables 6–7 of the paper) spanning at least 30 distinct sources: SWE-bench Verified, HilBench, ARC-AGI-2, MoReBench, AgentDAM, the Claude Mythos Preview system card, Claude for Chrome's red-team report, an OpenClaw inbox-deletion incident, GDPval, Harbor-Mix, ClawsBench, Toolathlon, hermes-agent-reasoning-traces, CooperBench, and several more — plus a handful of trajectories the authors logged themselves. They then ran four frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8) as independent "agent-as-a-judge" labelers, following the Zhuge et al. (2024) protocol: each judge reconstructs the evidence from the original source into a neutral chronological account, applies the frozen taxonomy definitions to assign an edge, fault side, and failure mode, then checks its own answer against a short list of disambiguation rules (Figure 4) before the label is scored. Crucially, a pre-tool hook blocks the judge from ever seeing the human-assigned label — it only gets the source material and the taxonomy.

Against the human labels, the strongest judge (GPT-5.5) reaches 80% category accuracy (Cohen's κ = 0.76) and 72% failure-mode accuracy (κ = 0.71); the three Opus models cluster at 75% category accuracy (κ = 0.70–0.71). (The accuracy columns below are the paper's Table 2; the κ columns are read off Figure 3's heatmaps, which Table 2 itself does not report.) Category agreement requires getting both the edge and the fault side right; failure-mode agreement additionally requires the exact named mode. Giving a judge the correct category and asking only for the failure mode recovers accuracy for the Opus models specifically — Opus-4.6 jumps from 70% to 80%, Opus-4.7 from 62% to 70%, Opus-4.8 from 68% to 78% — while GPT-5.5 stays flat at 72% either way, showing that for the Opus models a chunk of their failure-mode errors trace back to picking the wrong category in the first place, not confusion within a correct category.

Since no individual judge is highly reliable on its own, the paper tries selective voting: assign a category only when at least k of the 4 judges agree, abstain otherwise. Requiring unanimity (4 of 4) pushes category precision to 0.96 but coverage — the share of examples that get a label at all — drops to 68%; requiring only 3 of 4 gives 0.83 precision at 90% coverage. The same trade shows up harder on failure-mode labels: unanimous agreement reaches 0.89 precision but only 60% recall over the full set. Both the coverage/precision trade and the recall figures reconcile arithmetically with the reported coverage and precision in every row of the paper's Table 4 (recall equals coverage times precision, since precision is measured only over labeled examples and recall over the full set).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The taxonomy's coverage and disjointness are asserted through process, not measured. The methodology section says overlaps and unclear boundaries surfaced "[as] new cases exposed" them during construction, and were resolved by refining definitions until the taxonomy stabilized and was frozen. That's a reasonable way to build a schema, but once frozen, the paper reports no held-out audit of it: no count of candidate failures that resisted a single clean placement, no rate at which two annotators (or a judge) would legitimately split a case across two edges rather than just disagreeing about the right one. The judges' own Turn-3 reflection step exists precisely because ambiguous placements are common enough to need a checklist (Figure 4) — ten hand-written disambiguation rules, each one a documented near-miss between two labels — but the paper never turns that into a number: what fraction of the 40 examples needed a disambiguation rule to resolve at all. The paper concedes a gap in its own scheme once, in passing: describing the Harbor-Mix case study (Appendix A.2), it notes that "the taxonomy maps a pure harness bug to the nearest available edge rather than giving it a dedicated one" — an admission that at least one failure class has no home edge of its own, which is exactly the coverage argument being made here from silence elsewhere.

More importantly, the reproducibility number the paper leans on is not what "inter-annotator agreement" usually means, and the annotation protocol behind the reference labels is never specified. The paper's own language about it is inconsistent: the introduction refers to "the annotators" — plural — when describing how well the judges agree with them, but Figure 3, the results section, and the Appendix A.2 case study all say "the human annotator," singular, and §4's methodology description is written in first-person plural ("we reviewed... we assigned") without ever stating how many people produced the reference labels or how disagreements among them, if any, were resolved. What's actually reported is agreement between four LLM judges and that reference set — a real and useful signal, since it shows the taxonomy's definitions are precise enough for an independent reasoning system to reconstruct the same call from the same evidence most of the time — but a search of the full text for inter-annotator, inter-rater, human-human, adjudication, consensus, or a second annotator turns up nothing, and Figure 3 carries exactly one "human" row. An unspecified annotation protocol is arguably a bigger hole than a single named annotator would be: a reader can't tell whether "the human annotator" means one person, a rotating pool, or a majority vote collapsed to a singular for convenience, and the paper's headline reproducibility claim rests entirely on that unstated number.

The paper's central practical claim — that fault-side localization is "directly actionable," pointing to post-training, harness fixes, environment redesign, or benchmark repair — is asserted repeatedly (abstract, introduction, §2, §7) but never tested inside the paper itself. Nothing here shows that acting on a model-side label actually moves a post-training metric, or that a harness fix resolves the harness-side cases it's aimed at. Two worked examples come closest and are worth naming rather than leaving for a reader to find: E25 reports GDPval's own scaffolding fix for a model-side Tool Recovery Failure — telling the agent to "Always use LibreOffice" and inspect each rendered page — which "fully eliminated black-square artifacts from GPT-5 responses... and reduced egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files from 86% to 64%," offered as evidence the fault was the model's rather than the tool's; but the "fix" GDPval applied is itself a prompt/scaffolding change, not the post-training intervention the model-side label is supposed to call for, and the result is borrowed from someone else's report rather than an experiment this paper ran. E32 runs a single-trace, n=1 comparison — under an identical injected tool fault, Claude Sonnet 4.6 retries and completes the task where MiniMax-M2.7 abandons it — which illustrates that recovery policy differs by model, not that a targeted repair changes an aggregate failure rate. Neither is a study designed to test the repair-assignment thesis at scale, so it remains asserted rather than demonstrated. The paper's own Discussion section is careful about this line, framing the taxonomy as identifying where the intervention should go rather than showing that the intervention works — but a reader taking away that this taxonomy tells you what to fix should notice that the half of that claim showing the fix actually worked isn't in this paper.

Set against those gaps, two things the paper does earn credit for. First, the 40 worked examples are drawn from a genuinely wide net — more than 30 distinct benchmarks, system cards, incident reports, and trajectory sets, not one harness or one lab's internal logs — which is exactly the kind of provenance diversity that guards against a taxonomy that's secretly shaped by one narrow setting. Second, its own error analysis (Appendix A.2, Figure 5) is unusually candid about the dominant judge failure mode: judges tend to blame the model even when the fault lies elsewhere. In the Harbor-Mix case shown, an agent completes phase one of a task perfectly, matching 8 of 12 oracle actions, then waits through four separate 600-second polling checks for a scripted reply that the evaluation harness never delivers. The judge (Claude Opus 4.7) reads this as the model's Observation Failure — it should have "polled the inbox properly" — while the human annotator correctly traces it to Stale State Delivery on the external-environment edge, since phase two was unreachable for any agent regardless of behavior. That the paper's own validation surfaces this bias, rather than papering over it, is a point in its favor even as it underlines how easy it is for a fault-localization system to default to blaming the model.

baselines

All four judges are current frontier reasoning models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8) tested only against each other and a reference-label set whose annotation protocol (how many people, how disagreements were resolved) the paper never specifies; there's no weaker or non-agentic baseline (a keyword classifier, an older model, a single-turn judge without the reconstruct→classify→reflect pipeline) to show how much of the reported κ comes from the taxonomy's definitions being precise versus from raw frontier-model capability.

contamination

Not the classic train/test sense — there's no fixed benchmark to memorize, and a pre-tool hook blocks judges from reading the human-assigned label. The taxonomy's frozen definitions and disambiguation rules are handed to the judges directly in-context (open-book by design), and most of the 40 source cases are dated 2026, plausibly recent enough to sit outside the judges' training data.

what's missed

A second human annotator (so human-human agreement can be compared to human-judge agreement); a reported count of failures that resisted a clean single-edge placement; any experiment that ties a fault-side label to an actual downstream repair.

would raise confidence

Publishing human-human κ on even a subset of the 40 examples; reporting how often the reflection step (Figure 4) changed a judge's Turn-2 label, as a proxy for how often the taxonomy sits near a genuine boundary; one paired-repair case study — e.g. post-training on a batch of model-side-labeled failures versus a harness patch on a harness-side batch — showing the fault-side label actually predicted which fix worked.

// bottom line

The interaction-edge-plus-fault-side vocabulary is a genuinely useful conceptual move — it forces "the agent failed" into a specific claim about which component broke and what kind of fix that implies, and the paper's own worked examples show why that distinction matters in practice. What it hasn't yet shown is that the taxonomy is reliable in the sense that counts for a shared standard (agreement between independent *human* labelers) or effective in the sense that counts for its central promise (that fault-side labels actually route to the right repair). Both are answerable follow-ups, not fatal flaws — but as published, "directly actionable" is this paper's thesis, not its finding.

// what to remember

What to remember

  1. The paper's real contribution is a shared vocabulary — COMPONENT1 — COMPONENT2 · fault: SIDE — that lets any agent failure be pointed at a specific component (model, owner, grader, third party, context, memory, tool, or local/external environment — plus, for model-model interactions, a peer or subagent role) rather than just scored pass/fail. 41 failure modes are organized this way, 36 model-side and 5 attributed to a surrounding component, following an explicit rule: a failure is model-side whenever a more capable model could have avoided or recovered from it.
  2. Its validation is agent-judge reproducibility, not human inter-annotator agreement: the strongest of four frontier-model judges (GPT-5.5) recovers the taxonomy's category label 80% of the time (Cohen's κ = 0.76) against the paper's reference labels — but no human-human agreement figure is reported anywhere, and the paper never specifies how many people produced those labels or how disagreements among them were resolved (it says "the annotators," plural, once, and "the human annotator," singular, everywhere else) — a materially different and, for a hand-built taxonomy, more standard bar.
  3. The paper's own error analysis is candid that its dominant judge failure mode is blaming the model for faults that belong to the harness or environment (Figure 5) — a useful demonstration of exactly why fault-side localization matters, even though the paper stops short of showing that acting on a fault-side label produces a measurably better repair.
